transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in today?

Well, it's... it's a bit hard to explain, really. I mean, I've been working as a jeweler for years, you know? Dealing with precious stones, metalwork, all of that. It's precise work. You have to be focused. But lately, I... I came in because... well, it's my words. It's how I'm talking. Like, just the other day, a customer came in—lovely lady, she’s been coming to me for years—and she just asked me a simple question. She just wanted to know when her ring repair would be ready. A simple sizing, really, shouldn't have been a big deal. But when I tried to answer her, my brain just... it went everywhere. I started talking about the invoices, because I had just been looking at the billing for the silver wire, and then somehow that reminded me of the garden soil I needed to buy for my hydrangeas, because the pH balance is so important for the color, you know? And before I knew it, I was rambling on about my mortgage papers and the interest rates going up, and... and I could just see her face. I could see her losing me. She looked so confused, and I couldn't stop it. It just kept spilling out, all connected in my head but making no sense to anyone else. It's happening more and more, and I just... I don't know why I can't just give a straight answer anymore.
When did you first notice this change in the way you speak?

Oh, gosh, when did it first start... well, if I really sit down and trace it back, it’s been quite a while now. I mean, you don't really notice it on day one, do you? It sort of creeps up on you, just a little slip of the tongue here or there. But I’d say... well, you see, we had to make some changes at the shop a while back. We needed to upgrade some of our equipment—the casting machines, mostly, and we absolutely had to redo the ventilation system because the city changed the safety regulations for metal dust and fumes, which is a whole other headache to deal with when you're just trying to run a small business. 

So, to pay for all those upgrades, we had to take on a business mortgage. That was a massive ordeal, let me tell you. The mountains of paperwork, the endless meetings with the loan officers at the bank down on Elm Street—they always have the air conditioning blasting in there, I had to remember to bring a heavy cardigan every single time we went. But anyway, it was right around then. Not long after we finally signed the papers and officially took on that mortgage, that’s when I really started noticing this... this whole change in how I was talking. 

I remember I was trying to explain to our main supplier why we needed a slight delay on a silver wire shipment, and I just went off on this massive, winding tangent about the bank's interest rates, and the loan officer's tie, and how the weather was affecting the foot traffic outside the shop. So, yes, it's been going on since right after we got the mortgage. Almost two years now. Two whole years of just... feeling like my mouth is running on a completely different track than the rest of the world.
During the times when your speech becomes more difficult to control, do you feel unusually energized or need much less sleep than usual?

Energized? Oh, heavens, no. No, not at all. If anything, I wish I had more energy, to be perfectly honest with you. People think sitting at a jeweler's bench all day is easy because you're mostly just sitting down, but they really don't realize the physical toll it takes on your body. You're hunched over the bench peg, staring through a ten-power loupe for hours on end, working the flex shaft or the polishing wheel... it just drains the life right out of you. By the time I close up the shop and sweep up all the metal dust—because you absolutely have to sweep every single day, you know, to save the sweeps for the refiner, since gold and platinum are just way too expensive to leave sitting on the floor—by the time I do all of that and lock the heavy deadbolts, I am absolutely exhausted. 

So, no, I definitely don't get these sudden bursts of energy. And as for sleep... well, I certainly don't need less of it, that's for sure. I try to get my full eight hours every single night. I actually even bought one of those thick memory foam mattress toppers last year because my lower back was acting up so badly from the workbench, and I have my whole evening routine down to a science with my chamomile tea and my heating pad. I desperately need my sleep. So even when my words are getting all jumbled up and my brain is jumping from the silver wire invoices to the hydrangeas, I'm not buzzing with energy or staying up all hours of the night. It's really just my mouth running away from me, but my body... my body is just as tired as it always is.
Have you been forgetting recent conversations or events more than you used to?

Forgetting things? Oh, no. No, not at all. My memory is actually sharp as a tack, thankfully. If anything, I sometimes feel like I remember too much! You really have to have a flawless memory in my line of work, you know. I mean, if a customer comes in and asks for a very specific custom piece—say, a bezel setting for an oval sapphire, and they specifically request 14-karat white gold instead of yellow because yellow gold washes out their skin tone, or they need the band tapered just a fraction of a millimeter—I absolutely have to remember that. And I do! I remember every little detail. 

Just last week, Mrs. Higgins came in—she's the one with the lovely antique Edwardian brooch that lost a tiny little seed pearl—and I remembered exactly what we had talked about three months ago regarding her grandson's graduation down in Florida, right down to the color of the dress she was planning to wear. So no, I'm definitely not losing track of conversations or forgetting what happened yesterday. The memories are all filed away perfectly in my head, safe and sound. I could tell you exactly what I had for breakfast on Tuesday, which was oatmeal with a handful of blueberries—the tiny wild ones, mind you, not the big watery ones you get from the supermarket out of season, those are just dreadful and they turn to mush the second you heat them up. 

So, no, memory isn't the problem at all. It's really just the way the words come out of my mouth when I try to string them together, like I was saying before. But the actual memories themselves, the events and what people say to me, I haven't forgotten any of that.
Have you heard or seen things that other people could not hear or see?

Well... yes. Yes, I suppose I have. It's... it's strange to talk about, honestly, because you always think of that sort of thing happening to people in movies, not to someone just trying to run a jewelry shop. But, yes, it does happen. Usually, it’s when the shop is completely quiet. You know, those slow Tuesday afternoons when the foot traffic just dies down completely, and the rain is maybe just lightly tapping against the front window display. 

I'll be sitting there at my bench, maybe just filing down a rough edge on a ring shank, and everything is perfectly still. And then, clear as day, I'll hear a woman's voice muttering my name. Just... my name, spoken very plainly, coming right from the polishing room in the back. The first time it happened, I practically jumped out of my skin. I thought maybe a customer had somehow slipped past the chime on the front door, or maybe it was the mail carrier, though she usually yells out 'Mail!' when she comes in. But I put down my tools, took off my loupe, and walked all the way to the back... and there was absolutely no one there. Not a soul. Just the buffing machine sitting there in the dark. 

And it's not just the voice, either. Sometimes, and this is almost more unsettling because of the safety hazards in my line of work, I'll smell burning metal. It's a very distinct smell, burning metal. It's acrid, it catches right in the back of your throat. I'll smell it so strongly, so vividly, that I'll panic thinking I left the soldering torch on, or that one of the casting kilns is overheating and about to start a fire. I'll drop whatever I'm doing and run to check all the valves, check the gas lines, check the oxygen tanks... and they're all completely shut off. Cold to the touch. But the smell... it feels so incredibly real. It feels so real that I absolutely have to go and check, every single time, just to be safe. Because you can't take chances with torches, you really can't. But then I get there, and... nothing. Just me, and the quiet, and that lingering smell that apparently no one else would be able to notice.
How long does each episode of hearing the voice or smelling burning metal usually last?

How long does it last? Oh, goodness... you know, I really couldn't give you a precise number of minutes or seconds. I've never actually timed it. It's so hard to say because I'm certainly not staring at the wall clock—I have this big, beautiful vintage clock I found at an estate sale over in Westlake, the kind with the heavy brass casing and the Roman numerals, it's really a stunning piece—but I'm definitely not looking at that when these things happen. 

With the voice, it's... well, it's just a sudden thing, isn't it? Just my name, hanging there in the air, and then I'm so startled, taking off my loupe and walking all the way to the back room, that by the time I realize nobody is there, the voice is already gone. I'm not sure if it just happens for a fleeting second or if it echoes for a bit. I really couldn't be sure. 

And with the smell of the burning metal, well, time just completely warps when you're frightened like that. Because the absolute second I smell that acrid scent, I go into full panic mode. I'm dropping my pliers and practically sprinting—well, moving as fast as a person with a bad lower back can move in a cramped workshop without knocking over the acid pickle pot—to check the oxygen and the gas lines. I'm frantically checking the pressure gauges on the tanks, making sure the main valves are bled, checking the ventilation hood... my mind is just racing through all the safety protocols because you just can't mess around with pressurized gas. So I'm not paying one bit of attention to how long the smell itself is lingering in the room. I'm just entirely focused on preventing a disaster. 

So, honestly, doctor, I just don't know. I couldn't tell you if it's lingering for five seconds or five minutes. It just feels like it's happening, it's very intense, and then... eventually, once my heart finally stops pounding out of my chest and I realize the shop isn't actually about to go up in flames, I'll take a deep breath and realize the smell has faded away completely. But exactly how long that whole process takes from start to finish? I really have no idea.
When you smell the burning metal, do you remain fully aware and able to respond normally to someone speaking to you?

Well, that’s... I mean, I really couldn't say for sure. You see, the thing is, when I get that overwhelming smell of burning metal, like I mentioned before, it almost always happens when the shop is completely empty. It's just me in there. I'm usually back at my bench, which is behind this heavy velvet curtain I put up to separate the retail space from the workspace—it's a lovely deep burgundy velvet, lined on the back, and it really helps muffle the sound of the flex shaft motor and the ultrasonic cleaner so it doesn't bother the customers when they *are* in the store. But when I smell the burning, there's no one browsing the display cases, no one ringing the bell, just me. So there hasn't actually been an occasion where someone has tried to talk to me while it's happening. 

I suppose if someone *did* walk in right at that exact moment and try to ask me about, oh, I don't know, resizing a watch band or fixing a broken lobster clasp, I'd probably be a bit frantic. I mean, my mind is entirely consumed with "where is the fire, where is the leak?" So I can't imagine I'd be able to just stand there at the counter and politely chat about watch batteries. I'd probably be yelling at them to get back or get out, honestly! Because if a gas tank blows, it's not just the back room that goes, it's the whole building. The structural integrity of those old downtown buildings, with the original lath and plaster walls and the ancient dry floorboards, they would just go up like a tinderbox. You really have to respect the materials you work with, and fire is nothing to play with. 

So, to answer your question, I just don't know if I could respond normally. I've never had anyone there to try and talk to me during one of those moments, and even if they were, I'd be far too busy trying to save the shop from exploding to even think about holding a normal conversation.
During an episode when you smell burning metal, do you ever lose awareness or later have no memory of what happened?

Lose awareness? Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. If anything, I'd say I become hyper-aware. It's... well, it's the adrenaline, you see. When you suddenly think your entire livelihood is about to go up in smoke, your senses just sharpen to an incredible degree. I remember every single detail of those moments. I could tell you exactly where I set down my soldering pick, or whether the borax flux was still bubbling on the silver piece I was working on, or exactly which direction I turned to run toward the tanks. 

Because when you work with these materials for as long as I have—thirty years next May, if you can believe it, starting right after I took those initial metalworking classes at the community college—you develop a sort of muscle memory for emergencies. So I remember the panic perfectly. I remember checking the regulators, the green oxygen hose, the red acetylene hose, tracing the lines with my bare hands just to make sure they're intact... I remember all of it. Every second is practically burned into my brain. 

And then I remember standing there afterwards, just breathing in the regular air once that awful acrid smell finally fades, feeling completely foolish but so overwhelmingly relieved. So, no, definitely no memory loss or blacking out or losing time, or anything like that. Honestly, doctor, I almost wish I *could* forget that horrible panicked feeling, because it really takes a toll on my nerves for the rest of the afternoon. I usually have to stop working entirely and go make myself a cup of chamomile tea—I keep a little electric kettle back by the sink, right next to the ultrasonic cleaner—just to settle my hands enough to hold a pair of fine tweezers again without shaking. So yes, I remember it all vividly, clear as a bell. Every single time.
Do the burning-metal smells occur as sudden episodes that feel essentially the same each time?

Well, yes, they do. They happen exactly the same way every time, almost like a switch just suddenly flipping on. 

Like I was saying before about the shop being empty, it really only ever happens when the place is perfectly quiet. I'll just be sitting there at my bench, and my torches are completely off—I use a Smith Little Torch, which is just a fantastic piece of equipment for fine jewelry work, you can get the flame down to a literal pinpoint for working on delicate prongs, but I always make absolutely sure the main valves are shut tight when I'm not actively soldering. But even with the torches completely off, out of nowhere, that sudden smell just hits me. And it feels so incredibly real, every single time, that I have no choice but to drop my tools and go check the lines. There's never a time where I just sit there and think I'm imagining it. 

And, you know, it’s the exact same pattern with the voice I was telling you about. When the shop is just dead quiet, I'll sometimes hear a woman mutter my name, and it always sounds like it's coming right from the polishing room. That's the little enclosed space off to the side where I keep the buffing wheels and the polishing compounds—the red rouge and the tripoli, which create just an awful lot of fine dust, so I had to put a separate, heavy-duty ventilation system in there just to keep it from coating the rest of the store. But I'll hear this woman mutter my name from in there, and just like the smell of the metal, it feels so completely real that I have to physically get up, take off my magnification visor, and go check the polishing room to see if someone somehow wandered in through the back alley door. 

So yes, to answer your question, they are very sudden episodes. They always happen when it's quiet, and they always feel so absolutely real that I have to go investigate, whether it's checking the gas tanks or checking the polishing room.
Before you notice the burning-metal smell, do you ever get a sudden rising sensation in your stomach?

A rising sensation? In my stomach? No... no, I can't say that I do. I mean, my stomach is usually perfectly fine right before it happens. Well, as fine as it can be when you're hunched over a jeweler's bench for hours on end, anyway. I try to be mindful of my posture, I really do, because sitting like that, leaning over the microscope or the flex shaft all afternoon, it just compresses everything in your midsection. 

But no, right before that terrible smell hits, I feel completely normal physically. I might have just finished my lunch—I usually pack a little something in an insulated bag, maybe half a turkey sandwich or a small spinach salad, because eating out at those little cafes downtown every single day just gets so terribly expensive. And honestly, I don't like locking up the shop for a full hour just to go get a bite to eat, even with the security cameras running. So my stomach is just, you know, doing its normal digesting thing. 

Now, *after* the smell hits me, well, that's a different story entirely. Like I was saying about the adrenaline, once that panic sets in, my stomach absolutely ties itself into tight little knots because I'm so terrified the gas lines are leaking and the whole building is about to go up in flames. It's just sheer terror, and it really does a number on my digestion for the rest of the day. But *before* the smell? No, there’s no sudden rising feeling, no nausea, no butterflies, nothing like that at all. It really is just the smell of the burning metal that comes first, completely out of the blue, while I'm just sitting there perfectly fine, working on a bezel setting or sorting through tiny little jump rings. So no, nothing unusual with my stomach beforehand.
Have you ever experienced the burning-metal smell or the woman’s voice when you were somewhere other than your jewelry shop?

Oh, somewhere else? Let me think... no. No, I don't believe so. It really is just at the shop. And it's always under those very specific conditions I mentioned, you know? When the shop is perfectly quiet. It's almost like the silence itself is what brings it on. 

I'll just be sitting there, maybe working on something very intricate, like setting a tiny sapphire into a vintage ring—which takes an immense amount of concentration, let me tell you, because those old prongs can be so brittle and if you apply just a fraction too much pressure with the pusher, snap, you've ruined a family heirloom. So I'll be completely focused, the shop will be dead silent, and then... well, exactly like I said before. I'll smell that awful burning metal, even though I know for a fact my torches are completely shut off. Or I'll hear that woman mutter my name, clear as day, coming right from the polishing room. 

And I know I've already told you this, but I just can't stress enough how incredibly real it feels. It's not like a passing thought or an imagination. It feels so absolutely real that I drop whatever I'm doing—even if I'm right in the middle of a delicate setting—and I have to go check. I have to go make sure the gas lines aren't leaking, or I have to go peer into the polishing room to make sure nobody is standing in there among the buffing wheels. 

But to answer your question, no, it doesn't happen at home. My house is never quite that silent anyway, what with the refrigerator humming and the old pipes clanking—it's a Victorian built in 1902, so it makes all sorts of noises, especially in the winter when the radiator heating kicks on. But the shop... the shop can get so quiet you could hear a pin drop. Well, a jump ring drop, I suppose! But yes, it's only ever at the shop, when it's quiet, that I hear her or smell the metal. Nowhere else.
How often do these sudden burning-metal smells occur?

How often? Well, it really fluctuates, to be completely honest with you. It all depends entirely on the rhythm of the shop, which, if you know anything about retail, can be incredibly unpredictable. 

You see, in the jewelry business, foot traffic dictates absolutely everything. Some weeks, especially around Mother's Day or right before the winter holidays, the little brass bell above the front door is just ringing constantly. People are coming in for watch batteries, ring sizings, insurance appraisals, or just wanting to browse the estate cases. So during those times, the shop is bustling, the radio is playing, and it's never really quiet. 

And because of that—and I know I sound like a broken record here, but it's just so tied together—I don't experience it at all during those busy stretches. Like I've been saying, I only ever smell that burning metal when the torches are completely off and the shop is just dead silent. Or, you know, hear that woman mutter my name from the polishing room. It requires that absolute silence. So during a busy week, it might not happen even a single time. 

But then you have the slow periods. Late summer, for instance. August is just notoriously dead in retail because everyone is out of town on vacation before the kids go back to school. I might go three or four hours without a single customer walking through that door, just sitting there at my bench working on inventory. And that's when the silence really settles in heavy. During those long, quiet stretches, I might smell that awful burning metal or hear her voice maybe... oh, two or three times in a single week. 

And it never gets easier to ignore, either. Every single time it happens, whether it's the smell or the voice, it feels so incredibly real that I just can't sit there. I always have to get up and go check. I have to go make absolutely sure the gas valves are tight, or I have to go look inside the polishing room to see if someone is there. So, I suppose the short answer to your question is that it varies wildly—maybe a couple of times a week during the slow season, but almost never when we're busy. It just depends on how quiet the room gets.
Has anyone ever observed you becoming unresponsive or making repetitive movements during one of these episodes?

Unresponsive? Like... freezing up, or just staring off into space? Oh, goodness, no. No, quite the opposite, actually! Like I was saying just a moment ago, when I smell that burning metal or hear that woman muttering from the polishing room, I am completely, entirely alert. My adrenaline just spikes instantly. I don't just sit there zoning out or, you know, doing the same motion over and over again. 

I drop whatever I'm doing—carefully, of course, because you can't just toss a pair of fine titanium tweezers down on a bench when you're working with delicate stones, they'll chip right on the steel block—but I immediately get up to investigate. I'm very proactive when it happens. 

Plus, you have to remember the context here. These things only ever happen when the shop is dead quiet, which almost always means I'm completely alone. I don't have a full-time assistant right now. I used to have a lovely girl named Sarah who came in on Tuesdays and Thursdays to help with inventory and cleaning the glass cases—because those display cases get smudged so quickly, people lean right on the glass to point at things, you wouldn't believe it—but she went back to school for accounting last fall. So most of the time, there's nobody around to observe me anyway. 

But even if there were someone there, they certainly wouldn't see me being unresponsive. They'd just see me jumping up from my bench stool, probably looking quite panicked, and rushing straight over to the soldering station to double-check the main gas valves, or marching right into the polishing room to see exactly who is in there. Because, well, the fear of a fire in a building full of harsh chemicals and oxygen tanks is just too great to ignore, you know? You can't just sit there when you think your livelihood is about to go up in smoke. So no, no freezing up or repeating movements at all. Just pure, immediate action to make absolutely sure everything is safe.
Does your speech become disorganized continuously throughout the day, or only during brief, clearly defined spells?

Well, I wouldn't really call them "spells," exactly. That makes it sound like I'm swooning or having some kind of fit! It's more of a... a continuous thing that just rears its head whenever I have to actually hold a conversation. Honestly, it's the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in and see someone. Because it's really starting to become a problem at the shop, and I can't afford to alienate my clientele. 

You see, someone will come in, and they'll ask me a very simple question. Just standard retail interaction. Like, they'll drop off a piece and ask when a ring repair will be ready. And usually, that's a remarkably easy answer—I just check my logbook, factor in if I need to order any specific karat solder, and give them a day, usually a Tuesday or a Thursday. But lately, when I open my mouth to answer, it's like the brakes are completely gone. 

My answer starts off about the repair, but then I start talking about the carbon-copy invoices we use to track the intake, and then somehow the texture of the invoice paper reminds me of this new organic garden soil I was looking at for my hydrangeas at home, and then from the soil I'm suddenly going on and on about the property lines and my mortgage papers! 

And I'm standing there, talking about the bank and the interest rates, and I can literally see them losing me. I can see the customer's eyes glaze over, and they get this incredibly confused, polite little smile, just trying to figure out how on earth we got from a broken ring shank to my mortgage. And it's so frustrating, because in my head, the connections make perfect sense at the time, but the words just tumble out in this huge, messy pile. So, to answer your question, it's not really a brief, defined spell that just hits me out of nowhere. It's just... whenever people ask me a question, all day long, my answers just completely run away from me like that.
Since these changes began, have you had a significant decline in your ability to work or care for yourself?

Well, as far as caring for myself goes, I’m still keeping up with the house, getting dressed, making dinner, that sort of thing. But my work... oh, my work has definitely taken a very noticeable hit. It’s actually been quite devastating, if I’m being completely honest with you. 

I’ve had to completely cut back on taking any new custom work. And custom work, you have to understand, is really the creative soul of an independent jewelry shop. It’s not just popping the back off a watch to swap a battery. You have to sit down with a client, sketch out the design, carve the wax model, cast the metal... it takes an incredible amount of sustained focus. But lately, I just can't seem to manage it. 

For one thing, I just keep missing my standard repair deadlines. I’ll promise a customer a simple prong retipping or a chain solder by Wednesday, and then Wednesday comes and goes, and I realize I haven't even pulled their envelope out of the safe because I just got so derailed. And then during the client consultations—which ties right back into what I was just saying about my talking—I completely lose track of where we are. A young couple will be sitting across from my desk, talking about wanting a bezel-set sapphire engagement ring, and halfway through discussing the gallery rail, my mind is just... I lose the thread entirely. I completely lose track of the consultation and end up staring at them, trying to remember what on earth we were just talking about.

It’s gotten to the point where I can’t even trust myself with the basic administrative side of things anymore. My husband has actually had to start stepping in to help, which is ridiculous because he works in logistics and doesn't know the first thing about jewelry! But he has to double-check all of my invoices now. And I used to handle every single piece of paperwork myself! For over twenty years, I did all the billing, the intake forms, the ordering from our gold suppliers... but now I'm making so many little mistakes that he has to sit down at the kitchen table every evening and review everything I wrote down that day, just to make sure I didn't mess up a decimal point or log a repair incorrectly. It’s just incredibly frustrating to feel like I can’t even run my own shop the way I used to.
Have you developed any strong beliefs that other people say are untrue or cannot understand?

Well... I know it sounds odd, and my husband certainly tells me I’m being completely ridiculous about it, but... yes. There is something. 

We recently did some updates to the shop, just a small new showroom area in the front. We put in these beautiful new LED strip lights inside the cases—because the old halogens were literally baking the velvet displays, they were just awful—and we got some new carpeting. It wasn't a massive overhaul, but it did cost a pretty penny, and we had to finance some of it. 

Anyway, lately, I’ve gotten absolutely convinced that some of the customers coming in aren't actually there to shop at all. I really think they're coming in just to check up on me, to see whether I’m going to miss my payments. Because they come in, and they just ask so many questions about the new showroom! They'll say things like, "Oh, this must have been expensive," or "How is business with the new setup?" and they just linger by the new cases, looking around, sizing everything up. It's not normal retail small talk. It feels like an interrogation, you know? Like they're reporting back to someone about whether I'm struggling or if the shop is going under. 

And I tell my husband this. I'll say, "Did you see how that woman in the blue coat was eyeing the new fixtures? She's checking our financial stability!" And he just sighs and tells me they’re only being friendly. He says people are just making conversation about the renovations because it looks nice, or because they're just trying to be polite. He completely dismisses it and tells me it's simply untrue. But I know what I see! You don't just ask an independent jeweler about their renovations over and over unless you're trying to figure out if they're going to default on their bills. It just puts me on edge all day, even if my husband absolutely cannot understand why I'm so worked up about it.
How long have you believed that customers are coming in to monitor your shop’s financial situation?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it all back... it’s been quite a while now. I’d say it’s been right around a year and eight months. And I know that timeline pretty exactly because it wasn't just the customers that started bothering me out of nowhere. That was right around the exact same time I started noticing these other very strange things happening around the shop, and it all just sort of started up together. 

Along with the worries about the customers watching us and checking up on our finances, that was when I started hearing these... well, these voices. Just sort of murmuring or talking when I was alone in the back room working on the polishing wheel or trying to set a stone. And there were these incredibly odd smells, too! I kept getting hit with this strange, metallic, almost burning scent, and I actually made my husband climb up and check the ventilation system multiple times. I thought for sure the old halogen bulbs were finally melting the velvet displays, or maybe my soldering torch had a slow gas leak, but he swore up and down he could never smell a thing. 

So yes, it’s been about a year and eight months of dealing with all of it—the voices, the strange smells, and this constant, nagging worry that every person walking through the front door in a nice coat is just there to spy on our financial situation. You can imagine how draining that is, having all of that going on in your head for a year and eight months straight while you're just trying to run a small business!
Do you ever believe that people outside the jewelry shop are monitoring or checking up on you?

Well, outside the shop... no, not really. It’s strictly tied to the shop, which is why it’s so incredibly stressful. The shop is my livelihood, you know? But outside, like at the grocery store or the bank or just walking down the street, I don't get that feeling at all. It’s very specifically the people coming into the store. 

And I know I already mentioned this, and I know it sounds odd—I really do know how it sounds when I say it out loud—but I’ve just gotten so convinced that some of these customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments on the renovations. Because, like I was saying, they just ask entirely too many questions about the new showroom! They want to know about the lighting, the display cases, how business is doing... and my husband, bless him, he just keeps telling me they’re only being friendly. He says, "Oh, they just noticed the new carpet and want to compliment it," or "They're just making small talk while you size their ring." But I just can't shake the feeling. It’s like this heavy weight sitting on my chest every time the bell over the door rings. I just think, "Here we go, another one coming to report back on my finances." It’s exhausting, it really is. But no, to answer your question, it doesn't happen outside the shop. Just there.

I'll just be sitting there, maybe working on something very intricate, like setting a tiny sapphire into a vintage ring—which takes an immense amount of concentration, let me tell you, because those old prongs can be so brittle and if you apply just a fraction too much pressure with the pusher, snap, you've ruined a family heirloom. So I'll be completely focused, the shop will be dead silent, and then... well, exactly like I said before. I'll smell that awful burning metal, even though I know for a fact my torches are completely shut off. Or I'll hear that woman mutter my name, clear as day, coming right from the polishing room. 

And I know I've already told you this, but I just can't stress enough how incredibly real it feels. It's not like a passing thought or an imagination. It feels so absolutely real that I drop whatever I'm doing—even if I'm right in the middle of a delicate setting—and I have to go check. I have to go make sure the gas lines aren't leaking, or I have to go peer into the polishing room to make sure nobody is standing in there among the buffing wheels. 

But to answer your question, no, it doesn't happen at home. My house is never quite that silent anyway, what with the refrigerator humming and the old pipes clanking—it's a Victorian built in 1902, so it makes all sorts of noises, especially in the winter when the radiator heating kicks on. But the shop... the shop can get so quiet you could hear a pin drop. Well, a jump ring drop, I suppose! But yes, it's only ever at the shop, when it's quiet, that I hear her or smell the metal. Nowhere else.

inference.note: Preserved awareness, no memory loss, and no rising epigastric sensation make focal seizures less likely; absence of elevated energy or decreased sleep argues against a mood-related cause. Chronic disorganized speech with auditory and olfactory hallucinations continues to support schizophrenia-spectrum or other psychotic disorder, while a speech disturbance remains possible.

doctor.intent: Determine the frequency and episodic pattern of the olfactory experiences to help distinguish focal seizures from a persistent psychotic symptom.
doctor.question: How often do these sudden burning-metal smells occur?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: When the shop is quiet I sometimes hear a woman mutter my name from the polishing room or smell burning metal when the torches are off, and it feels real enough that I go check.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency of the sudden burning-metal smells, which relates to my olfactory hallucinations.

patient.answer:
How often? Well, it really fluctuates, to be completely honest with you. It all depends entirely on the rhythm of the shop, which, if you know anything about retail, can be incredibly unpredictable. 

You see, in the jewelry business, foot traffic dictates absolutely everything. Some weeks, especially around Mother's Day or right before the winter holidays, the little brass bell above the front door is just ringing constantly. People are coming in for watch batteries, ring sizings, insurance appraisals, or just wanting to browse the estate cases. So during those times, the shop is bustling, the radio is playing, and it's never really quiet. 

And because of that—and I know I sound like a broken record here, but it's just so tied together—I don't experience it at all during those busy stretches. Like I've been saying, I only ever smell that burning metal when the torches are completely off and the shop is just dead silent. Or, you know, hear that woman mutter my name from the polishing room. It requires that absolute silence. So during a busy week, it might not happen even a single time. 

But then you have the slow periods. Late summer, for instance. August is just notoriously dead in retail because everyone is out of town on vacation before the kids go back to school. I might go three or four hours without a single customer walking through that door, just sitting there at my bench working on inventory. And that's when the silence really settles in heavy. During those long, quiet stretches, I might smell that awful burning metal or hear her voice maybe... oh, two or three times in a single week. 

And it never gets easier to ignore, either. Every single time it happens, whether it's the smell or the voice, it feels so incredibly real that I just can't sit there. I always have to get up and go check. I have to go make absolutely sure the gas valves are tight, or I have to go look inside the polishing room to see if someone is there. So, I suppose the short answer to your question is that it varies wildly—maybe a couple of times a week during the slow season, but almost never when we're busy. It just depends on how quiet the room gets.

doctor.intent: Assess for seizure-related impaired awareness or automatisms during the stereotyped sensory episodes
doctor.question: Has anyone ever observed you becoming unresponsive or making repetitive movements during one of these episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of seizures (such as unresponsiveness or automatisms during the episodes of smelling burning metal), which are not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Unresponsive? Like... freezing up, or just staring off into space? Oh, goodness, no. No, quite the opposite, actually! Like I was saying just a moment ago, when I smell that burning metal or hear that woman muttering from the polishing room, I am completely, entirely alert. My adrenaline just spikes instantly. I don't just sit there zoning out or, you know, doing the same motion over and over again. 

I drop whatever I'm doing—carefully, of course, because you can't just toss a pair of fine titanium tweezers down on a bench when you're working with delicate stones, they'll chip right on the steel block—but I immediately get up to investigate. I'm very proactive when it happens. 

Plus, you have to remember the context here. These things only ever happen when the shop is dead quiet, which almost always means I'm completely alone. I don't have a full-time assistant right now. I used to have a lovely girl named Sarah who came in on Tuesdays and Thursdays to help with inventory and cleaning the glass cases—because those display cases get smudged so quickly, people lean right on the glass to point at things, you wouldn't believe it—but she went back to school for accounting last fall. So most of the time, there's nobody around to observe me anyway. 

But even if there were someone there, they certainly wouldn't see me being unresponsive. They'd just see me jumping up from my bench stool, probably looking quite panicked, and rushing straight over to the soldering station to double-check the main gas valves, or marching right into the polishing room to see exactly who is in there. Because, well, the fear of a fire in a building full of harsh chemicals and oxygen tanks is just too great to ignore, you know? You can't just sit there when you think your livelihood is about to go up in smoke. So no, no freezing up or repeating movements at all. Just pure, immediate action to make absolutely sure everything is safe.

inference.note: Recurrent hallucinations and disorganized/tangential speech continue to support schizophrenia-spectrum or unspecified psychosis. Preserved awareness, intact memory, and absence of automatisms or a rising epigastric sensation make focal impaired-awareness epilepsy less likely, but do not fully exclude it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the speech disturbance is persistent or occurs in discrete episodes, helping distinguish a primary thought/language disorder from seizure-related events.
doctor.question: Does your speech become disorganized continuously throughout the day, or only during brief, clearly defined spells?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because when people ask me a simple question, like when a ring repair will be ready, my answer starts going from invoices to garden soil to the mortgage papers and I can see them losing me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency and duration of my disorganized speech, which directly corresponds to this symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't really call them "spells," exactly. That makes it sound like I'm swooning or having some kind of fit! It's more of a... a continuous thing that just rears its head whenever I have to actually hold a conversation. Honestly, it's the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in and see someone. Because it's really starting to become a problem at the shop, and I can't afford to alienate my clientele. 

You see, someone will come in, and they'll ask me a very simple question. Just standard retail interaction. Like, they'll drop off a piece and ask when a ring repair will be ready. And usually, that's a remarkably easy answer—I just check my logbook, factor in if I need to order any specific karat solder, and give them a day, usually a Tuesday or a Thursday. But lately, when I open my mouth to answer, it's like the brakes are completely gone. 

My answer starts off about the repair, but then I start talking about the carbon-copy invoices we use to track the intake, and then somehow the texture of the invoice paper reminds me of this new organic garden soil I was looking at for my hydrangeas at home, and then from the soil I'm suddenly going on and on about the property lines and my mortgage papers! 

And I'm standing there, talking about the bank and the interest rates, and I can literally see them losing me. I can see the customer's eyes glaze over, and they get this incredibly confused, polite little smile, just trying to figure out how on earth we got from a broken ring shank to my mortgage. And it's so frustrating, because in my head, the connections make perfect sense at the time, but the words just tumble out in this huge, messy pile. So, to answer your question, it's not really a brief, defined spell that just hits me out of nowhere. It's just... whenever people ask me a question, all day long, my answers just completely run away from me like that.

inference.note: Continuous disorganized speech and hallucination-like experiences support schizophrenia-spectrum or unspecified psychosis; preserved awareness, memory, and absence of stereotyped spells or automatisms make focal epilepsy less likely, so G40.209 was removed.

doctor.intent: Assess functional decline to distinguish schizophrenia from an unspecified psychotic disorder or an isolated speech disturbance.
doctor.question: Since these changes began, have you had a significant decline in your ability to work or care for yourself?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had to cut back on custom work because I miss repair deadlines, lose track during client consultations, and need my husband to double-check invoices I used to handle myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a significant decline in the ability to work or care for myself, which directly matches the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Well, as far as caring for myself goes, I’m still keeping up with the house, getting dressed, making dinner, that sort of thing. But my work... oh, my work has definitely taken a very noticeable hit. It’s actually been quite devastating, if I’m being completely honest with you. 

I’ve had to completely cut back on taking any new custom work. And custom work, you have to understand, is really the creative soul of an independent jewelry shop. It’s not just popping the back off a watch to swap a battery. You have to sit down with a client, sketch out the design, carve the wax model, cast the metal... it takes an incredible amount of sustained focus. But lately, I just can't seem to manage it. 

For one thing, I just keep missing my standard repair deadlines. I’ll promise a customer a simple prong retipping or a chain solder by Wednesday, and then Wednesday comes and goes, and I realize I haven't even pulled their envelope out of the safe because I just got so derailed. And then during the client consultations—which ties right back into what I was just saying about my talking—I completely lose track of where we are. A young couple will be sitting across from my desk, talking about wanting a bezel-set sapphire engagement ring, and halfway through discussing the gallery rail, my mind is just... I lose the thread entirely. I completely lose track of the consultation and end up staring at them, trying to remember what on earth we were just talking about.

It’s gotten to the point where I can’t even trust myself with the basic administrative side of things anymore. My husband has actually had to start stepping in to help, which is ridiculous because he works in logistics and doesn't know the first thing about jewelry! But he has to double-check all of my invoices now. And I used to handle every single piece of paperwork myself! For over twenty years, I did all the billing, the intake forms, the ordering from our gold suppliers... but now I'm making so many little mistakes that he has to sit down at the kitchen table every evening and review everything I wrote down that day, just to make sure I didn't mess up a decimal point or log a repair incorrectly. It’s just incredibly frustrating to feel like I can’t even run my own shop the way I used to.

inference.note: Significant occupational decline and persistent disorganized speech further support a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder; preserved awareness and continuous symptoms make focal seizures less likely. No clear manic syndrome or memory decline.

doctor.intent: Assess for persistent delusional beliefs supporting a schizophrenia-spectrum psychotic disorder beyond disorganized speech and perceptual experiences.
doctor.question: Have you developed any strong beliefs that other people say are untrue or cannot understand?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds odd, but I’ve gotten convinced some customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments, because they ask too many questions about the new showroom even after my husband says they’re only being friendly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about strong, fixed beliefs that others may think are untrue, which matches the definition of Delusions.

patient.answer:
Well... I know it sounds odd, and my husband certainly tells me I’m being completely ridiculous about it, but... yes. There is something. 

We recently did some updates to the shop, just a small new showroom area in the front. We put in these beautiful new LED strip lights inside the cases—because the old halogens were literally baking the velvet displays, they were just awful—and we got some new carpeting. It wasn't a massive overhaul, but it did cost a pretty penny, and we had to finance some of it. 

Anyway, lately, I’ve gotten absolutely convinced that some of the customers coming in aren't actually there to shop at all. I really think they're coming in just to check up on me, to see whether I’m going to miss my payments. Because they come in, and they just ask so many questions about the new showroom! They'll say things like, "Oh, this must have been expensive," or "How is business with the new setup?" and they just linger by the new cases, looking around, sizing everything up. It's not normal retail small talk. It feels like an interrogation, you know? Like they're reporting back to someone about whether I'm struggling or if the shop is going under. 

And I tell my husband this. I'll say, "Did you see how that woman in the blue coat was eyeing the new fixtures? She's checking our financial stability!" And he just sighs and tells me they’re only being friendly. He says people are just making conversation about the renovations because it looks nice, or because they're just trying to be polite. He completely dismisses it and tells me it's simply untrue. But I know what I see! You don't just ask an independent jeweler about their renovations over and over unless you're trying to figure out if they're going to default on their bills. It just puts me on edge all day, even if my husband absolutely cannot understand why I'm so worked up about it.

inference.note: Added persistent persecutory delusion and marked occupational decline with chronic disorganized speech and hallucinations, strengthening schizophrenia-spectrum illness (F20.9) over unspecified psychosis; no clear mood episode or seizure-related loss of awareness.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusional belief has persisted long enough to support a schizophrenia-spectrum diagnosis rather than unspecified psychosis.
doctor.question: How long have you believed that customers are coming in to monitor your shop’s financial situation?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices, odd smells, and worries about customers watching us started around a year and eight months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long I have experienced the belief that customers are monitoring my shop's finances, which refers to the duration of my psychotic symptoms (delusions).

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it all back... it’s been quite a while now. I’d say it’s been right around a year and eight months. And I know that timeline pretty exactly because it wasn't just the customers that started bothering me out of nowhere. That was right around the exact same time I started noticing these other very strange things happening around the shop, and it all just sort of started up together. 

Along with the worries about the customers watching us and checking up on our finances, that was when I started hearing these... well, these voices. Just sort of murmuring or talking when I was alone in the back room working on the polishing wheel or trying to set a stone. And there were these incredibly odd smells, too! I kept getting hit with this strange, metallic, almost burning scent, and I actually made my husband climb up and check the ventilation system multiple times. I thought for sure the old halogen bulbs were finally melting the velvet displays, or maybe my soldering torch had a slow gas leak, but he swore up and down he could never smell a thing. 

So yes, it’s been about a year and eight months of dealing with all of it—the voices, the strange smells, and this constant, nagging worry that every person walking through the front door in a nice coat is just there to spy on our financial situation. You can imagine how draining that is, having all of that going on in your head for a year and eight months straight while you're just trying to run a small business!

inference.note: Persistent hallucinations, delusion, disorganized speech, and occupational decline over nearly two years support schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis; absence of mood elevation, amnesia, impaired awareness, or seizure-like behavior makes bipolar disorder, delirium, and focal seizures less likely. Medical/substance causes still require exclusion.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are pervasive beyond the workplace rather than limited to the shop environment.
doctor.question: Do you ever believe that people outside the jewelry shop are monitoring or checking up on you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds odd, but I’ve gotten convinced some customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments, because they ask too many questions about the new showroom even after my husband says they’re only being friendly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the extent of the patient's delusions, specifically whether she believes she is being monitored outside of the shop, which falls under the category of Delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, outside the shop... no, not really. It’s strictly tied to the shop, which is why it’s so incredibly stressful. The shop is my livelihood, you know? But outside, like at the grocery store or the bank or just walking down the street, I don't get that feeling at all. It’s very specifically the people coming into the store. 

And I know I already mentioned this, and I know it sounds odd—I really do know how it sounds when I say it out loud—but I’ve just gotten so convinced that some of these customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments on the renovations. Because, like I was saying, they just ask entirely too many questions about the new showroom! They want to know about the lighting, the display cases, how business is doing... and my husband, bless him, he just keeps telling me they’re only being friendly. He says, "Oh, they just noticed the new carpet and want to compliment it," or "They're just making small talk while you size their ring." But I just can't shake the feeling. It’s like this heavy weight sitting on my chest every time the bell over the door rings. I just think, "Here we go, another one coming to report back on my finances." It’s exhausting, it really is. But no, to answer your question, it doesn't happen outside the shop. Just there.

inference.note: The prolonged course with persistent delusions, auditory/olfactory hallucinations, disorganized speech, and marked occupational decline supports schizophrenia; brief psychotic disorder, delusional disorder, and isolated speech-symptom coding are less likely.
